content.p: In the small hours of 21 May 1938, in a mountain hamlet on the border of Okayama and Tottori prefectures, a young man cut the village's power line, strapped flashlights to his head and went from house to house with a shotgun, a sword and an axe. By the time he walked out of Kaio an hour and a half later, 30 people were dead and three more were wounded. Some of the dead were children. The first was his own grandmother, who had raised him. At about ten that morning he shot himself on a ridge above the valley.

The man was Mutsuo Toi, then 21 by the way age is counted outside Japan and 22 by the Japanese reckoning of 1938. He was never tried, because he died before he could be questioned. The case is known in Japan as the Tsuyama thirty-murders incident, after the nearest city. It is described in the sources as the worst killing by a lone attacker in Japanese history, and the questions it left behind, about tuberculosis, shame and the closed life of a village, have been argued over ever since.
content.h2: A clever boy in a closed valley
content.p: Toi was born in March 1917. According to Unseen Japan, he lost both parents to tuberculosis while still a toddler, and he and his older sister were handed to their grandmother. When he was six the household moved to her home hamlet of Kaio, a narrow valley between mountains. The family had an income and some land, and he was formally head of the household because women could not be.

He did well at the village school and was thought gifted, though classmates later remembered a pessimism behind his gentle smile and he had no close friends. Pleurisy at fourteen began a run of illnesses that left him weak and withdrawn. A Bunshun excerpt from Ishikawa's research describes a slim, pale youth in a place where most men were dark and muscular, and says women found him attractive. The same account says he was reputed to have had relationships with more than ten women of the hamlet, many of them older and married.

That sits against a village custom that writers on the case keep returning to: yobai, or night visiting, in which men slipped into women's houses after dark. Unseen Japan notes that by the 1930s the practice was officially discouraged, that survivors were angry when police asked whether it still went on, and that some of Toi's contemporaries said it was still common among local youth. How much of the story of his sexual life is solid, and how much was later repetition, is one of the points the case has never settled.

Everything changed, according to the accounts Unseen Japan relies on, at the military conscription examination in 1937. Toi hoped to be passed as fit. The doctor told him he had tuberculosis, and he was given the lowest grade. Unseen Japan adds that sources differ on whether he already knew before the examination or had it confirmed there.

The disease carried a heavy stigma. Unseen Japan quotes the postwar psychopathologist Kazuo Nakamura as saying that in the area tuberculosis was widely believed to be hereditary and that people covered their mouths and noses when they passed an infected house. Ishikawa, writing for Gendai Business, says that after the examination some women of the hamlet, who had earlier had relations with Toi, exposed his night visits to others and mocked him, and he judges that their ridicule was a major cause of the crime.

Toi became suspicious and shut himself away. He pursued women in the hamlet, Unseen Japan reports, and neighbours began to see him as dangerous and shunned him. He took out a hunting licence, bought a gun and spent his days practising in the mountains. His grandmother, alarmed, went to the police after seeing him put a powder in her soup; he said it was medicine. Police searched the house, took away swords and knives and cancelled his licence, but Unseen Japan says he got more weapons from an acquaintance.

Money was part of the picture. Ishikawa writes that Toi borrowed 600 yen in January 1938, which paid for his preparations, and that his house and land were mortgaged. When police searched the house after the killings they found 66 sen.

Around 5 p.m. on 20 May, Unseen Japan reports, Toi climbed a pole and cut the line that fed the hamlet. Nobody reported the outage. He dressed in a high-collared black uniform with gaiters and work boots, tied a headband with a flashlight at each temple and hung a bicycle lamp from his neck. Ishikawa and Bunshun list a sword and two daggers at his belt, a modified nine-shot Browning shotgun and an axe. A 1938 Tokyo Asahi dispatch, quoted by Bunshun, gave the gun as a ten-shot, 12-gauge hunting piece. A film review elsewhere calls it a Remington; the sources do not agree on the make.

His first victim was his grandmother, asleep in the house they shared. Ishikawa describes how he struck her neck with the axe several times and that she bit the cloth over her pillow in her last moments. The Asahi dispatch put the start at about 1:40 a.m.; other accounts say 1:30. Bunshun's excerpt notes that writers have guessed he chose the axe to avoid noise or to spare his sword's edge, and Ishikawa suggests there was a more personal reason, which is left unresolved.

He then moved through the hamlet. Ishikawa's account for Gendai Business has him enter the neighbouring house first, then a second, then a third, usually killing with one or two shots. He says people Toi resented most were hit repeatedly, children included. One victim, a young woman in the third house, was six months pregnant, which is why some writers speak of thirty-one victims. The Okayama police history, quoted in Bunshun, describes villagers hearing shots draw nearer, people pressing against doors that were shot through, and a young couple killed side by side in one bedding.

Not everyone was targeted. Unseen Japan reports that Toi spared one father, telling him he had never spread rumours about him, and that he told an elderly woman, before shooting her at close range, that her son had married into a family he held a grudge against. She survived and could later describe the night. A father in another house ran to the nearest police post and was the first to report the attack. The police history says the killer ran off around three in the morning.

Toi wrote three farewell notes. A Japanese rendering of one is reproduced on RENOTE; the gist below is translated here from the Japanese. He apologised to his grandmother and to his sister, and said he had wept at the coldness and pressure of society during four years of illness and at having so few relatives to love him. Society, he wrote, should show more sympathy to tuberculosis patients. He named the woman whose arrival in Kaio had prompted him to act that day, adding that she had got away, and he named men he thought should be removed from the world. Bunshun's excerpt notes that traces of preparation date from months earlier, so the visit of two women to the hamlet that week may have brought the date forward rather than caused the plan.

Toi left the hamlet and stopped at a farmhouse, where, in Unseen Japan's telling, he asked for pen and paper and told the son to mind his studies. He climbed the slope near Arasaka Pass and shot himself in the chest. Money Gendai and the Asahi report put the time at about 10:30 a.m. Bunshun adds that for hours the people of the valley feared he was loose in the mountains with his guns, and that schools were closed until his death was known.

The Asahi evening edition of 21 May carried the headline of 32 people killed or wounded, quoted in Bunshun. The same dispatch, as Bunshun prints it, called the grandmother his mother, which Bunshun marks as an error. Ishikawa and later writers give 30 dead and three wounded.

The size of the loss depended on the hamlet. Ishikawa gives its population as 111. In his Gendai Business piece he says that 10 of its 22 households, plus one in a neighbouring village, were attacked, and that nearly a third of the villagers died; in his Money Gendai piece he gives 11 of 22 households and more than a quarter of the villagers. Unseen Japan says three households were wiped out entirely and four were left with a single survivor. Thirty deaths out of 111 is a little over a quarter, so the figures do not all fit together, and the discrepancy is among those the sources leave open.

The funerals were held jointly. Ishikawa writes that they were conducted on 23 May from 3 a.m. to 7 a.m., with firefighters burying households where no family remained. Twenty-seven bodies were placed there. Neither Toi nor his grandmother was allowed in the joint ceremony, and one young woman's body went back to her home village. The same day a decision not to prosecute the dead suspect was taken, and many bereaved families, he says, felt cheated by it. Grave markers in the hamlet still carry the date of 21 May 1938.

Families lost farmland, about six hectares, and silkworms they could no longer tend; relatives and neighbours took them over with support from the village office. Toi's own house was sold three months later for 50 yen, which went to his creditors, and demolished in November, Ishikawa says. Unseen Japan, however, writes that the house stood rotting until it was pulled down in 2015, and Bunshun says only that the original building is gone. Which account is right on this point is not clear from the pages.

Within the hamlet, Unseen Japan writes, those whose families had been left untouched were looked on with suspicion, as if they had been in league with the killer, while the bereaved struggled to farm with fewer hands. Most survivors eventually moved away and the subject became taboo. Bunshun's Arata Koike notes that national papers did cover the case, though much less than its scale would suggest, and that one postwar chronicle wrongly dated it to late 1937 and put the toll at over forty.

A woman Ishikawa interviewed in 2010 under a pseudonym, aged 94, is described as the woman Toi was said to have been fixated on. She said she did not want to remember or talk; five of her family were killed. Once his behaviour changed, she said, she avoided Toi, even stepping into the rice paddies to keep away from him on the road. On the night she ran to a neighbour's house, and the old man who sheltered her was killed too.

The detailed police findings stayed out of reach for decades. Ishikawa wrote that the Justice Ministry's report on the case was unavailable for years after the war, so that writers of the 1970s and the years after, among them Seicho Matsumoto and Akira Tsukuba, worked from other material, and rumours spread, even to the point that some people admired the killer. Ishikawa traced the report to a university library in the western United States, which the publisher Futami Shobo names as the Hoover Institution. His final book, published in October 2024 after his death in 2022 at 57, reprints the full document, titled as an incident of 33 persons killed or wounded in Nishi-Kamo village.

In 1949 the mystery writer Seishi Yokomizo used the case as the base for his novel Yatsuhaka-mura, The Village of Eight Graves. Unseen Japan says his killer's costume was taken directly from Toi's. Films followed, including the 1983 Village of Doom by Noboru Tanaka, which Grimoire of Horror describes as a graphic dramatisation. A manga on the case by Ryoko Yamagishi changes the killer's name, Real Sound notes, and takes some invention in the conversations.

The Indian Express, listing such events after a 2016 knife attack that killed 19, called the Tsuyama killing the only one in decades with a higher toll. Unseen Japan says it was regarded as the worst by a single person worldwide until 1982, and that some commentators now read it alongside later grievance-driven attacks, though it also cautions that whether Toi should be called an early example is disputed.
